content_html:
Ten years ago, I began writing a series about how we could move toward humane tech. Over the next year, I tried to get the people who build technology to look honestly at what the industry was becoming, while there was still time to change it. As you may be aware, that didn’t quite succeed.

Every once in a while, I’ll see people passing around links to some of those pieces, specifically to call out a couple of predictions that I made with the genuine hope that I would turn out to be wrong.

In March of 2016, I wrote:

In a time of rising inequality, those who profit greatly while massively disrupting the stability of ordinary people tend to not be seen very kindly. The oil and steel barons of the past were seen as high tech innovators and valuable job creators for a while, until their excesses and abuses earned them a serious backlash.

That post was framed around a simple warning: unless people in tech became more self-critical, the industry’s leaders would come to be seen as the new robber barons. And then about six months later, in “How do we reform tech?”, I tried to say what was at stake if we didn’t:

The single biggest threat to the long-term health and growth of the tech sector is the backlash that could be caused by tech’s worst abuses and excesses.

Well, here we are

At the time, plenty of people in the industry read those as the worries of a pessimist. That was also the era when tech’s most powerful voices (the investors who would have you believe that writing checks matters more than writing code) began a systematic campaign to undermine all criticism. They began to position journalists as their enemies, and said that anyone who was critical of tech leaders having absolute, unaccountable power over the economy and society was an enemy of progress, someone who hated innovation. It did not matter if, as was often the case, those of us who were being critical were actually creating more innovations than the financiers who were pushing this big lie about tech criticism.

It may be hard to remember now, but a decade ago, tech was still treated as the unalloyed good guys. Founders and CEOs were the job creators and the inventors of the future, and politicians of every stripe were happy to be photographed next to tech’s biggest names. Media stories were framed around how parents would want their kids to be “the next Zuckerberg”.

As you may be aware, that is not the world we live in now.

We’ve arrived at the reckoning I was describing, and it’s worse than we’d have imagined. Tech’s most powerful voices have embraced authoritarianism wholesale, enthusiastically adopted an openly corrupt form of cronyism as central to their business models, and aggressively gone to war against their own workers (and labor in general) as part of a campaign to ensure that they’re never held accountable for any of the harms or wrongs that they cause. The result? A political environment where the largest tech companies and their founders are seen, accurately, as completely unregulated and unaccountable powers that inflict their will upon people across the world without consent or consideration.

The part I most wish I had gotten wrong is the last bit of the first quote. I said the robber barons of the past got their backlash “until their excesses and abuses earned them” one. I was hoping that the industry would choose to reform itself before it got to that point. That was the entire point of all the writing and public speaking I did in that era.

But unfortunately, I failed. We weren’t able to stop the abuses. And now, the tech tycoons who’ve led us here are about to find out just how angry the world is at their abuses, their excesses, and their obvious attempts to show the rest of society that they are above the law and any moral or ethical rules.

Things are not going to go the way that they think.

Just how bad it gets is going to depend on how quickly they understand just how poorly they’ve read the room. As I keep pointing out, hundreds of thousands of tech workers have lost their jobs; when I wrote about it at the beginning of the year, it was half a million — now it’s closer to a million.

None of those ordinary tech workers lost their jobs because they were having inappropriate relationships with a subordinate, or because they had bribed the President of the United States with tens of millions of dollars, or because they had a sexual relationship with a foreign asset that compromised national security. But they can see that someone can get away with all of those harms, and still have a job paying unimaginable riches, even while decent people are struggling to get by. They will not miss the lesson that’s being taught.

What history teaches us

I don’t take any pleasure in having called this one. If anything, it makes the case for the rest of what I wrote back then stronger, not weaker. The reforms I was asking for in 2016 are no more radical now, and they are far more urgent. And the people inside the industry who still care about doing right by the world have a much stronger argument to push for change than they did a decade ago, because the alternative is being lumped in with the tycoons who are feverishly working to become the most hated people in the world.

If you’ve been waiting for a sign that it’s time to speak up, you’re out of excuses. The backlash that’s coming is going to be extreme. And I know that because all we have to do is look at the last time there was a class of robber barons who abused their power to this degree. Those tycoons probably controlled less of the economy, and had less of an obvious impact on people’s day-to-day lives, and yet the reason they ended up funding all those libraries and museums we see today is because they spent enough years dodging bombing attacks and assassination attempts that they finally realized something had to change. I would love to see today’s tycoons invest in the public sphere in order to rehabilitate their image, but they’ve already shown that their preference is to double down on shamelessly acting like they’re untouchable.

Perhaps they really are above any accountability. We will certainly find out.

Everyone is going to have to pick a side on today’s robber barons. I think they’re in such an isolated and extreme cultural and media bubble that they genuinely don’t understand how wildly unpopular they are. But for ordinary tech workers, and the people affected by the decisions that these tycoons make, now is the time to make clear which side you’re on. The lessons of the past are clear: you will not want to side with the people who are willing to shamelessly abuse others and assume that the chickens will never come home to roost.
